rationale: This qualitative study (based on ethnographic fieldwork from 2008 to 2017, 30 semi-structured interviews with politicians, administrators, and engineers, and documentary analysis of CAG audits and DJB records) examines multiple co-central legal and governance mechanisms shaping water access in Delhi: (1) institutional_structure_coordination (primary), including Delhi's hybrid city-state intergovernmental oversight structure, Chief Minister political control over the DJB, internal divisions between IAS administrators and engineers, fragmented measurement practices, and blurred jurisdictional boundaries routing water across WTPs, 9 E&M divisions, 22 civil divisions, and assembly constituencies; (2) discretion_accommodation, via street-level bureaucratic arbitrariness and political patronage by MLAs, MCD Councilors, and local DJB engineers who allocate discretionary funds for tankers/tubewells, turn valves, respond selectively to complaints, or overlook illegal tubewells and defunct meters; and (3) eligibility_status_documentation, via Section 9.1.A of the 1998 DJB Act barring formal piped connection rights to informal settlements on unauthorized land. Outcomes span multiple co-central families: effective_access (primary: stark disparities in water quantity in lppd, service intermittency/hours of flow, and unreliable tanker vs piped deliveries), primary_connection (exclusion of informal settlements from central grid connections), and administrative_outcome (institutional illegibility, flawed water/loss accounting, and obscured bureaucratic accountability).
